title: Are we all Martians?
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck open with announcements about a New York trip: an October 12, 2012 "Stuff You Should Know Day" in the five boroughs, a live podcast during Comic Con, and a trivia night with a celebrity team. They then cover panspermia, the idea that life arrived on Earth from space, starting with Lord Kelvin's 1870s proposal that seed-bearing meteorites brought life, and Svante Arrhenius's 1906 coinage and microbe-based version. They discuss Mars meteorites (including the 1984 ALH84001 meteorite and its heat-exposure study at Caltech), NASA estimates of Martian rocks hitting early Earth, bacteria surviving space exposure, gun-launch and centrifuge-style acceleration tests, and ancient bacteria revived from amber and salt crystals. Then they promote the Sweet Sixteen horror fiction reader-voting bracket, and close with a listener email about auto-parts invoice fraud and a sign-off.
topics: Stuff You Should Know New York trip

segments.summary: Hosts banter about the show and announce Stuff You Should Know Day in New York City on October 12, 2012, a live podcast during Comic Con, and a trivia night with a celebrity team.

segments.title: Panspermia and Lord Kelvin
segments.summary: Introduction to the origin-of-life debate: abiogenesis (RNA-based) versus panspermia. Panspermia was proposed by Lord Kelvin, who suggested seed-bearing meteorites, possibly from Mars, brought life to Earth. Svante Arrhenius coined the term in 1906 and later argued microbes travel via starlight or radiation pressure rather than inside rocks.

segments.title: Viking probes and Mars meteorites
segments.summary: The Viking probes measured Mars atmosphere, which matched gases trapped in Mars meteorites found on Earth. Researchers identified 104 meteorites from Mars and showed rocks can travel from Mars to Earth and survive intact.

segments.title: ALH84001 and heat survival
segments.summary: The ALH84001 meteorite, found in Antarctica's Allan Hills, was studied for possible microbial fossils. Caltech researchers used its magnetic signature to show it never got hotter than about 104 degrees Fahrenheit, so microbes could survive. NASA scientists estimated many Martian rocks hit early Earth, and the inner solar system likely allows life exchange, while interstellar odds are very low.

segments.title: Bacteria surviving space and launch
segments.summary: Lynn Rothschild and Rocco Mancinelli exposed halophile bacteria on a satellite, and about ten survived two weeks. Gerda Horneck's group fired bacteria in bullets and sent Bacillus subtilis into orbit for six years, where spores formed protective shells and about thirty survived.

segments.title: Ancient bacteria in amber and salt crystal
segments.summary: Bacteria isolated from a bee gut preserved in roughly 40-million-year-old amber were still alive, and bacteria from a 250-million-year-old salt crystal were also reported alive. The hosts conclude a Martian origin is possible but not probable and raise the question of where life began.
topics: 250 million year old salt crystal bacteria

segments.title: Listener email on auto parts invoice fraud
segments.summary: A former counter employee at an auto repair shop describes discovering that a coworker altered and photocopied invoices to steal money. The hosts comment on whether this counts as white collar crime, and they close with contact information and sign-off.
